newsitem.title: UK: Commodity prices mixed on U.S. inflation fears.
newsitem.headline: Commodity prices mixed on U.S. inflation fears.

text.p: Commodities prices were mixed as equities fell on Thursday in reaction to a surprise decline in U.S. unemployment figures as a sign of renewed inflationary pressure.

Fears that a hotter U.S. inflation outlook would lead to higher interest rates took the recent flush out of equities particularly while the largely speculator-driven oil market turned round as Wendesday's buyers took their profits.

But most of the commodity markets set their own agenda with aluminium which hit a 2-1/2 year low on Wednesday slipping further but managing to stay above the psychologically signifiant $1,300 per tonne level.
Copper was firmer while the precious metals led by silver continued slow but steady progress away from recent low points.
"Silver closed impressively, breaking the downtrend," a dealer said as silver managed to close over $5.00 at $5.01 per ounce for the first time since September 19.
Gold's progress however was less than spectacular as it added barely 50 cents through the day to close at $381.95.
"Gold is running into selling at around $382. There's not a lot it can do at this point," a dealer said.
On the London Metal Exchange (LME) three month aluminium futures slumped to $1,305 a tonne on Thursday from $1,323 at the close on Wednesday, before bouncing to $1,332 by late afternoon.
The market opened the year at $1,700.
"There has been some heavy selling out of the U.S. recently," said Macquarie Equities analyst Adam Rowley, responding to floor trader talk of selling from U.S. banks.
Consumer demand throughout the year has fallen well short of expectations due to buyers drawing on their own stocks.
This phase is thought to be close to completion, according to analysts.

Copper prices perked up on dealers' forecasts that LME warehouse stocks would fall again on Friday continuing the trend establish early last month which has reduced invetories to their lowest level in nearly a year.
Red metal futures were indicated at $1,955 per tonne at $1620 GMT around $30 ahead of Wedensday's close.
Of the soft commodites, London cocoa futures were most prominent with a gain of around nine stg on the day after good consumer buyting found few willing sellers.
The March contract closed at 1,014 stg.

Coffee futures trimmed early losses on late investment fund buying but the January contract still ended down $17 at $1,471 and sugar edged above the day's lows in late business to be $1.00 ahead on $323.00 at 1620.
